title: Counting successes
objectives: Derive the binomial distribution from independent trials
Find the mean $np$ and variance $np(1 - p)$ of a binomial count
Recognise when the binomial does not apply

screens.title: Counting successes
screens.prose: A strategy takes three trades. Each one wins with chance 0.6, whatever the others do. We will find the chance of every possible number of wins.
Each path through the tree is one way the three trades can turn out. The trades are independent, so each branch keeps the same chances.
screens.question: Tap the last branch of every path with exactly one win.

hints.text: Read each path from left to right and count its wins.
The win can come first, second or third.
Win, loss, loss is one path. Loss, win, loss and loss, loss, win are the other two.

feedback.correct: Three paths have exactly one win: the win can sit in any of the three trades.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count the wins on each path you tapped, and find every path with exactly one.

byKey.one-order: You tapped only win, loss, loss. The single win could also come second or third.
byKey.at-most: You included loss, loss, loss. That path has no wins, not one.
byKey.w-w-w: Win, win, win has three wins.
byKey.w-w-l: Win, win, loss has two wins.
byKey.w-l-w: Win, loss, win has two wins.
byKey.l-w-w: Loss, win, win has two wins.
byKey.l-l-l: Loss, loss, loss has no wins.

explain.text: You found three paths: the one win sits in trade 1, 2 or 3. Each path has one factor of 0.6 and two of 0.4. So all three paths have the same chance, $0.6 \times 0.4^2 = 0.096$.

screens.prose: Let $X$ be the number of wins in the three trades. The leaves now show each path's chance. Paths with the same number of wins share a chance.
screens.question: Fill in the chance of each number of wins.

hints.text: Paths with the same count are separate outcomes, so their chances add.
The two-win paths each have chance 0.144.
Multiply the number of paths by the chance of one path: for one win, $3 \times 0.096 = 0.288$.

feedback.correct: Paths times the chance of one path, for every count.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. For each row, multiply the number of paths by the chance of one path.

explain.text: Each row is (number of paths) times (chance of one path). The four chances add to 1, because every path has some number of wins. This list of chances is the distribution of $X$.

screens.prose: The number of wins in $n$ independent trials, each won with chance $p$, has a **binomial distribution**, written $X \sim \text{Bin}(n, p)$. Your table was $\text{Bin}(3, 0.6)$. Slide $n$ and $p$ and watch the shape.
screens.question: Set $p = 0.5$ and try a few values of $n$. What do you see?

options.why: That is the shape for a small $p$, such as 0.2. At $p = 0.5$ a win and a loss are equally likely, so neither end is favoured.
You may have pictured each count as one outcome. Middle counts have many more paths: $\binom{n}{k}$ peaks in the middle.

hints.text: Compare the bar for 0 wins with the bar for $n$ wins.
At $p = 0.5$, swapping every win for a loss gives a path with the same chance.

feedback.correct: At $p = 0.5$ the chart is a mirror image about $n/2$. Any other $p$ tilts it.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Set the win chance to 0.5 and compare the two ends of the chart.

explain.text: At $p = 0.5$, $k$ wins and $k$ losses have the same chance, so the bars mirror about $n/2$. With $p$ above 0.5 the bulk moves right and a tail trails left. With $p$ below 0.5 it is the other way round.

screens.prose: Now five trades, each won with chance 0.6. A path with 3 wins has chance $0.6^3 \times 0.4^2 = 0.03456$. Drawing the tree would take 32 paths.
screens.question: How many of the 32 paths have exactly 3 wins?

hints.text: A path is fixed by which trades are wins.
Choose which 3 of the 5 trades are the wins. Order does not matter.
That is $\binom{5}{3} = \tfrac{5 \times 4 \times 3}{3 \times 2 \times 1}$.

feedback.correct: $\binom{5}{3} = 10$ ways to choose which trades win.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count the ways to choose which 3 of the 5 trades are wins.

byKey.five: You counted the trades. A path is a choice of which 3 trades win.
byKey.ordered: $5 \times 4 \times 3 = 60$ counts ordered picks. Picking trades 1, 2, 4 in any order gives the same path, so divide by $3! = 6$.
byKey.three: You counted the wins. Different paths put those 3 wins in different trades.

explain.text: A path is fixed by the set of trades that win, so there are $\binom{5}{3} = 10$ of them. Each has chance 0.03456. So $P(X = 3) = 10 \times 0.03456 = 0.3456$.

screens.prose: Shrink to one trade, $n = 1$. Then $X$ is 1 for a win and 0 for a loss. This one-trial binomial is called a **Bernoulli** variable.
screens.question: What is $\text{Var}(X)$ for this single trade?

hints.text: Find $E[X]$ and $E[X^2]$ first.
$X$ is 0 or 1, so $X^2 = X$ and $E[X^2] = E[X] = 0.6$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Use $\text{Var}(X) = E[X^2] - E[X]^2$, with $X^2 = X$.

byKey.mean: 0.6 is $E[X]$, the mean. The variance subtracts the squared mean from $E[X^2]$.
byKey.loss: 0.4 is the chance of a loss, $1 - p$. Multiply it by $p$.

explain.text: Because $X$ is 0 or 1, $X^2 = X$, so $E[X^2] = p$. Then $\text{Var}(X) = p - p^2 = p(1 - p) = 0.24$. At $p = 0$ or $p = 1$ this is 0: the trade's result is certain.

screens.prose: Four trades, each a fair coin flip: $p = 0.5$. A colleague says the chance of exactly 2 wins is $0.5^2 \times 0.5^2 = 0.0625$.
screens.question: What is $P(X = 2)$?

options.why: That is the chance of one path, such as win, win, loss, loss. Five other orders also give two wins.
You took 2 out of 4 as the chance. That is the share of trades won, not the chance of exactly 2 wins.
You counted two paths, such as WWLL and LLWW. The wins can sit in any 2 of the 4 trades: 6 paths.

hints.text: How many paths have exactly 2 wins?
The bar for 2 wins is the tallest, so it must be well above 0.0625.
$\binom{4}{2} = 6$ paths, each with chance $0.5^4 = 0.0625$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count the paths with 2 wins, then multiply by one path's chance.

byKey.one-path: You used the chance of a single path and forgot $\binom{4}{2} = 6$. Six different orders give two wins.

explain.text: The colleague found one path's chance and stopped. Six orders give two wins: WWLL, WLWL, WLLW, LWWL, LWLW and LLWW. So $P(X = 2) = 6 \times 0.0625 = 0.375$, six times the colleague's answer.

screens.prose: Now the general case: $n$ independent trials, each a success with chance $p$. We want $P(X = k)$, the chance of exactly $k$ successes.
screens.question: Put the lines of the derivation in order.

lines.text: One path with $k$ successes and $n - k$ failures has chance $p^k(1 - p)^{n - k}$: independent chances multiply.
Every such path has that same chance: only the order of the factors changes.
There are $\binom{n}{k}$ such paths: choose which $k$ of the $n$ trials are successes.
Paths are separate outcomes, so add their chances: $P(X = k) = \binom{n}{k}p^k(1 - p)^{n - k}$.

hints.text: Start with one path, as you did on the tree.
Before you count paths, you need to know they all have the same chance.
One path, all paths equal, count them, add.

feedback.correct: One path, every path the same, count the paths, add.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Start with the chance of one path, then explain why counting paths is enough.

byKey.add: The sum needs the count and the shared chance first, so it comes last.
byKey.count: Counting paths only helps once you know every path has the same chance.

explain.text: This is your table, written for any $n$ and $k$. With $n = 3$, $k = 2$, $p = 0.6$ it gives $3 \times 0.36 \times 0.4 = 0.432$. The two conditions are a fixed number of trials and independent trials with the same $p$.

screens.prose: Now the mean and variance for 20 trades. Write $X = I_1 + \cdots + I_{20}$, where $I_i = 1$ if trade $i$ wins. Linearity gives $E[X] = 20p$. Each $\text{Var}(I_i) = p(1 - p)$, from the single trade. The trades are independent, so their variances add.
screens.question: Write $\text{Var}(X)$ in terms of $p$.

widget.label: Variance of the number of wins

hints.text: How many indicator variances are you adding?
Independent variables: $\text{Var}(I_1 + \cdots + I_{20}) = \text{Var}(I_1) + \cdots + \text{Var}(I_{20})$.
Twenty copies of $p(1 - p)$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Add the 20 indicator variances, each $p(1 - p)$.

byKey.mean: $20p$ is the mean. Each indicator contributes $p(1 - p)$ to the variance, not $p$.
byKey.scaled: $400p(1 - p)$ is $\text{Var}(20 I_1)$: one trade scaled by 20. Twenty independent trades partly cancel, so you add 20 variances instead.
byKey.one: That is one trade's variance. There are 20 independent trades to add.

explain.text: Independence makes every covariance zero, so the 20 variances add: $\text{Var}(X) = 20p(1 - p)$. In general $E[X] = np$ and $\text{Var}(X) = np(1 - p)$. Without independence the covariances stay and this sum is wrong.

screens.prose: A strategy wins 55% of its trades, independently. Next week it will take 20 trades. Its number of winners is $X \sim \text{Bin}(20, 0.55)$.
screens.question: What is the standard deviation of the number of winning trades? Give 3 decimal places.

hints.text: Find the variance $np(1 - p)$ first.
The standard deviation is the square root of 4.95.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Take the square root of $np(1 - p)$.

byKey.variance: 4.95 is the variance. The standard deviation is its square root.
byKey.mean: 11 is the mean, $np$. The spread around it is $\sqrt{np(1 - p)}$.

explain.text: The mean is $20 \times 0.55 = 11$ wins and the standard deviation is $\sqrt{4.95} \approx 2.225$. A week of 9 or 13 wins is ordinary noise. Judging the strategy on one week tells you little.

screens.prose: How likely are 15 or more wins out of 20 for this strategy? That needs six terms of the formula. Build the whole distribution as a list, then sum its tail. Use `math.comb` and plain Python.
screens.question: Complete `binom_pmf(n, p)` so that item `k` of the list is $P(X = k)$.

widget.starter:
from math import comb

def binom_pmf(n, p):
    """[P(X = 0), ..., P(X = n)] for X ~ Bin(n, p)."""
    return [... for k in range(n + 1)]

# The chance of 15 or more wins in 20:
# sum(binom_pmf(20, 0.55)[15:])
widget.solution:
from math import comb

def binom_pmf(n, p):
    """[P(X = 0), ..., P(X = n)] for X ~ Bin(n, p)."""
    return [comb(n, k) * p**k * (1 - p)**(n - k) for k in range(n + 1)]

tests.call: sum(k * q for k, q in enumerate(binom_pmf(20, 0.55)))

widget.how: Check runs 9 hidden tests, including $p = 0$ and $p = 1$. Each number is accepted within a relative error of 1e-9.

hints.text: Each item is $\binom{n}{k}p^k(1 - p)^{n - k}$.
In Python that is `comb(n, k) * p**k * (1 - p)**(n - k)`.
Replace the `...` with that expression; the list comprehension runs it for every `k`.

feedback.correct: The list is the whole distribution. Its tail from 15 sums to about 0.0553.
feedback.generic: Some tests failed. Each item should be `comb(n, k) * p**k * (1 - p)**(n - k)`.

byKey.error: Your code stopped with an error. Check that the `...` is replaced by an expression.

explain.text: Summing the list from index 15 gives $P(X \ge 15) \approx 0.0553$. So a skill-free week of 15 wins happens about once in 18 weeks at this win rate. The list also sums to 1 and has mean 11, two checks worth keeping.

screens.prose: A lender holds 50 loans. Each defaults this year with chance 0.02, independently of the others. The number of defaults is $\text{Bin}(50, 0.02)$, with mean 1.

state.caption: Defaults in a book of 50 loans

screens.question: What is the chance the book has no defaults at all this year?

hints.text: No defaults means every one of the 50 loans survives.
Each loan survives with chance 0.98, independently.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. All 50 loans must survive, each with chance 0.98.

byKey.mean-one: A mean of 1 is an average over many years. More than a third of years have no default at all.
byKey.one-loan: 0.98 is the chance one loan survives. All 50 must survive.
byKey.rate: 0.02 is one loan's default chance. You want the chance that none of the 50 default.

explain.text: All 50 loans survive with chance $0.98^{50} \approx 0.3642$. The binomial needs independence, and in a recession defaults move together. Then bad years with many defaults are far likelier than $\text{Bin}(50, 0.02)$ says.

ideas: The number of successes in $n$ independent trials, each with chance $p$, is $\text{Bin}(n, p)$.
Every path with $k$ successes has chance $p^k(1 - p)^{n - k}$, and $\binom{n}{k}$ paths have $k$ successes.
Indicators give $E[X] = np$; independence gives $\text{Var}(X) = np(1 - p)$.

formula.name: Binomial distribution
formula.note: For $k = 0, 1, \ldots, n$. With $n = 1$ it is a Bernoulli variable.

summary.trap: One path's chance is not the answer: multiply by $\binom{n}{k}$. And the trials must be independent.

quiz.prose: Four independent trades each win with chance 0.5.
quiz.question: What is the chance exactly one of them wins?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count the paths with one win, then multiply by one path's chance.

byKey.one-path: That is one path's chance. The single win can come in any of the 4 trades.
byKey.share: 0.5 is one trade's win chance, not the chance of exactly one win in four.

explain.text: The win can be trade 1, 2, 3 or 4: $\binom{4}{1} = 4$ paths. Each has chance $0.5^4 = 0.0625$. So the chance is $4 \times 0.0625 = 0.25$.

quiz.prose: Ten funds all hold a large position in the same stock. Each loses money on a given day with chance 0.4. Let $X$ be the number of funds that lose money tomorrow.
quiz.question: Is $X \sim \text{Bin}(10, 0.4)$?

options.text: No: the funds move together, so the trials are not independent

options.why: You checked $n$ and $p$ but not independence. One move in the shared stock hits every fund at once.

options.text: Yes, as long as every fund has the same chance
options.why: The same $p$ is needed, but it is not enough. The trials must also be independent.

options.text: No, because 0.4 is only an estimate
options.why: An estimated $p$ is a separate worry. The model fails here because the funds' results are linked.

feedback.correct: A shared position links the outcomes, so the binomial does not apply.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Check every condition for a binomial, including independence.

explain.text: The binomial needs independent trials. Funds holding the same stock tend to lose on the same days. So $X$ is often 0 or 10, far more than $\text{Bin}(10, 0.4)$ predicts.

quiz.prose: A desk takes 100 independent trades, each winning with chance 0.3.
quiz.question: What is the variance of the number of winning trades?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Use $\text{Var}(X) = np(1 - p)$.

byKey.mean: 30 is the mean, $np$. The variance also multiplies by $1 - p$.
byKey.sd: 4.583 is the standard deviation, $\sqrt{21}$. The question asks for the variance.
byKey.losses: 70 is the mean number of losses, $n(1 - p)$.

explain.text: Each trade is an indicator with variance $0.3 \times 0.7 = 0.21$. The trades are independent, so 100 of them add to 21. The standard deviation is $\sqrt{21} \approx 4.58$ trades.

quiz.prose: You can choose the win chance $p$ of each of 10 independent trades.
quiz.question: Which $p$ makes the variance of the number of wins largest?

options.why: At $p = 1$ every trade wins, so $X = 10$ always and the variance is 0.
Rare wins make the count small and steady: $10 \times 0.1 \times 0.9 = 0.9$.

options.text: It is the same for every $p$
options.why: You may have kept only $n = 10$. The variance $10p(1 - p)$ changes with $p$.

feedback.correct: $p(1 - p)$ is largest at $p = 0.5$, where it is 0.25.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compare $10p(1 - p)$ for the options.

explain.text: $\text{Var}(X) = 10p(1 - p)$, and $p(1 - p)$ peaks at $p = 0.5$ with value 0.25. So the largest variance is 2.5. At $p = 0$ or $p = 1$ the count is certain and the variance is 0.
